title: Task 2 — Opinion & Discussion Essays
summary: These two types look similar and trip up thousands of candidates for the same reason: a discussion essay is not an opinion essay. Get the difference clear, and you'll stop losing easy Task Response marks to a structural mix-up.

seo.title: IELTS Task 2 Opinion & Discussion Essays: Models | Vidaara
seo.description: How to write IELTS opinion (agree/disagree) and discussion essays — the key structural difference, step-by-step plans and two band-9 model essays.

objectives: Tell an opinion prompt apart from a discussion prompt at a glance
Keep a consistent position across a whole agree/disagree essay
Give both views AND your own opinion in a discussion essay
Study two band-9 models and copy what makes them work

blocks.html:
Opinion and discussion essays are the two most common Task 2 prompts, and they're the two most often confused. On the surface both ask what you think about an issue. Underneath, they demand different things — and mixing them up is one of the easiest ways to cap your Task Response score at 5 or 6 when your English deserves more.

Here's the short version. An opinion essay (agree/disagree) wants your position and your reasons for it. A discussion essay wants a fair account of two sides and your own view. The trap is writing a one-sided argument when the question asked you to discuss both sides, or forgetting to state your own opinion when the question specifically asked for it.

Opinion (Agree / Disagree)Discussion (Both views + opinion)
Signal wording"To what extent do you agree or disagree?""Discuss both views and give your own opinion."
What the examiner wantsYour position, defendedA fair look at both sides, plus your position
Body 1First reason supporting your viewView A, explained sympathetically
Body 2Second reason supporting your viewView B, explained sympathetically
Where your opinion livesEverywhere — the whole essay argues itStated in the introduction and conclusion (and woven into whichever view you favour)
Fatal mistakeSitting on the fence — no clear stanceDescribing both sides but never giving your own opinion

Opinion essays: pick a lane and stay in it

The instruction "to what extent do you agree or disagree?" is an invitation to commit. You have three honest options: fully agree, fully disagree, or partly agree (agree with reservations). All three can score band 9 — what matters is that your position is clear and consistent from the introduction to the conclusion.

The most common self-inflicted wound here is hedging. A candidate writes an introduction leaning one way, a first body paragraph arguing that way, then a second body paragraph arguing the opposite way with equal force — and by the conclusion the examiner genuinely cannot tell what the writer believes. That reads as an unclear position, and Task Response drops. If you want to acknowledge the other side, do it as a brief concession, then return firmly to your line.

blocks.title: Planning an opinion essay
items: Decide your stance first. Agree, disagree, or partly agree — pick one before you brainstorm, so every idea pulls in the same direction.
Find two reasons for that stance. Two distinct supporting reasons become your two body paragraphs. If you're partly agreeing, one paragraph can be the concession and one the main reason.
Attach an example to each. A real trend, a plausible scenario, a named field — concrete detail is what turns a claim into an argument.
State the position twice. Once in the introduction (clearly, no hedging) and once, reworded, in the conclusion. The examiner should never doubt where you stand.

blocks.html:
Discussion essays: be fair, then be honest

The phrase to watch is "and give your own opinion." It's easy to spend both body paragraphs faithfully explaining view A and view B, feel you've done a thorough job, and completely forget to say what you think. That single omission is enough to hold Task Response down, no matter how good the rest is.

The cleanest structure is one body paragraph for each view, explained sympathetically enough that a supporter of that view would nod along — then your own opinion made explicit in the introduction and again in the conclusion. Whichever view you personally favour, let that come through in the depth and confidence of the paragraph you write for it.

blocks.title: In a discussion essay you MUST give your own opinion
blocks.html: "Discuss both views and give your own opinion" is two instructions, not one. Discussing both sides fairly but never stating your own view is the single most common discussion-essay error, and it caps Task Response — often at band 6 for an otherwise strong script. Put your opinion in the introduction, reinforce it in the conclusion, and make sure a reader could quote it back to you in one sentence.

blocks.title: Planning a discussion essay
items: Identify the two views. The prompt hands them to you. Name them plainly so you don't blur them together later.
Decide your own opinion up front. You'll need it in the introduction, so choose which view you lean toward before you start writing.
One paragraph per view. Body 1 explains the first view with a reason and example; Body 2 does the same for the second. Present each fairly, even the one you disagree with.
Make your opinion unmistakable. State it in the introduction, and in the conclusion say clearly which view you find more convincing and why.

blocks.html:
Model 1 — Opinion (agree/disagree)

Read this one for how a single, unhedged position runs cleanly through every paragraph. Notice the writer never argues against their own side; the whole essay pushes one way.

blocks.title: Band-9 opinion essay
blocks.html:
Prompt: Some people think that governments should spend money on public services rather than on the arts, such as music and theatre. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

It is sometimes claimed that public money is better directed towards essential services than towards artistic pursuits like music and theatre. While I understand the appeal of prioritising hospitals and schools, I largely disagree with this view, because the arts deliver both economic and social returns that make them a wise use of public funds rather than a luxury.

The first reason is economic. A thriving arts sector is not a drain on the budget but a generator of income and employment. Theatres, galleries and music venues draw tourists, sustain thousands of jobs from performers to caterers, and revive city districts that would otherwise decline. Edinburgh's annual festival, for example, transforms the city each summer and returns far more to the local economy than the public grants that help sustain it. Cutting arts funding to protect other services can therefore be a false economy, removing revenue that supports those very services.

The second reason is social, and to my mind more important. The arts shape a society's identity and mental wellbeing in ways that hospitals and roads cannot. Community choirs, local theatre groups and free public concerts give people shared experiences and a sense of belonging, and there is growing evidence that participation in the arts improves mental health and reduces isolation. Withdrawing this funding would strip ordinary people — not just the wealthy — of access to culture, deepening the very social problems that public services then have to treat.

In conclusion, although essential services clearly deserve strong funding, I disagree that the arts should be sacrificed to pay for them. Because artistic activity brings genuine economic and social benefits, sustaining it is a sound investment rather than an indulgence.
annotations: The introduction states a clear position ("I largely disagree") after a brief, honest concession — the examiner knows the stance immediately.
Both body paragraphs argue the SAME side; the writer never switches to defend the opposing view, which keeps the position consistent throughout.
The concession ("While I understand the appeal...") is handled in a single clause, then the essay returns firmly to its line — the right way to acknowledge the other side without going off-position.
A specific, real example (Edinburgh's festival) anchors the economic argument instead of a vague generalisation.
The conclusion re-states the position in new words and links back to both reasons — a tidy, decisive ending.

blocks.html:
Model 2 — Discussion (both views + opinion)

Here the job is different: give each view a fair paragraph, then make your own opinion impossible to miss. Watch where the writer's opinion appears — introduction and conclusion, plainly stated.

blocks.title: Band-9 discussion essay
blocks.html:
Prompt: Some people believe children should start formal schooling at a very young age, while others think they should begin later. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Opinions differ on when children ought to begin formal education. Some argue that an early start gives children a valuable academic head start, while others maintain that a later start protects the play-based learning young children need. Having weighed both positions, I believe a later start is more beneficial for most children.

Those who favour early schooling point to the pace at which young minds absorb information. Children who begin structured lessons at four or five, the argument runs, master reading, writing and numeracy sooner, and arrive at later stages of education already ahead. In countries where formal instruction starts early, supporters note, children can be reading fluently before the age of six. From this perspective, delaying school simply wastes years in which the brain is at its most receptive.

The opposing view holds that very young children learn best through play, not formal instruction, and that pushing them into desks too soon can do harm. Advocates point to Finland, where children do not start formal schooling until age seven yet consistently achieve strong educational outcomes. In these systems, the early years are spent developing social skills, curiosity and physical confidence — foundations that make later academic learning more effective, not less. An early academic start, they warn, can breed anxiety and dull a child's natural love of learning.

In my view, the second position is the stronger one. While early literacy is appealing, the evidence that a later, play-based start produces confident, resilient learners without any long-term academic cost is difficult to dismiss. I therefore believe children benefit most from beginning formal schooling later, once they have built the social and emotional foundations that formal learning depends on.
annotations: The writer's own opinion appears in the introduction ("I believe a later start is more beneficial") — satisfying the 'give your own opinion' instruction from the very first paragraph.
Each body paragraph is devoted to one view and explains it sympathetically, so both sides get a genuine hearing rather than a straw-man version.
A concrete comparison (early-start countries vs. Finland at age seven) grounds each side in a real-world reference.
The conclusion doesn't just summarise — it re-commits to the writer's opinion and says clearly why, closing the loop the introduction opened.
Signposting language ("Those who favour...", "The opposing view holds...", "In my view...") keeps the two views and the personal opinion cleanly separated, which lifts Coherence.

blocks.title: The one-sentence test
blocks.html: Before you hand in either essay type, try to state your position in a single sentence out loud. For an opinion essay you should be able to say "I think X because A and B." For a discussion essay, "Side one says this, side two says that, and I lean toward ___." If you can't finish that sentence from your own essay, the examiner won't be able to either — go back and make your position explicit.

blocks.title: Next: the practical question types
blocks.html: Opinion and discussion cover a large share of exam prompts, but not all of them. Next we tackle the more procedural types — problem–solution, advantages–disadvantages, and two-part questions — including the notorious "outweigh" verdict trap that quietly sinks so many scripts.

faqs.q: What's the difference between an opinion essay and a discussion essay?
faqs.a: An opinion (agree/disagree) essay asks you to take one position and defend it, so the whole essay argues your side. A discussion essay asks you to explain both views fairly AND state your own opinion. The wording gives it away: 'to what extent do you agree?' is opinion; 'discuss both views and give your own opinion' is discussion.

faqs.q: Can I partly agree in an opinion essay?
faqs.a: Yes. Fully agreeing, fully disagreeing, and partly agreeing are all valid and can all reach band 9. What matters is that your position is clear and consistent throughout — a partial position must still be a definite one, not fence-sitting.

faqs.q: Do I have to give my opinion in a discussion essay?
faqs.a: Always, when the prompt says 'give your own opinion' — which discussion prompts do. Explaining both sides without stating your own view is the most common discussion-essay mistake and it caps your Task Response score. Put your opinion in the introduction and reinforce it in the conclusion.

faqs.q: Where should my opinion go in a discussion essay?
faqs.a: State it in the introduction so the examiner knows your stance early, and restate it clearly in the conclusion. You can also let it show in the depth and confidence of the body paragraph covering the view you favour, but the introduction and conclusion are essential.
